name: Ammon (Lot's son)
title: Ben-Ammi – Ancestor of the Ammonites
summary: Ben-Ammi was the son of Lot and his youngest daughter, conceived after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. After the disaster, Lot and his two daughters took refuge in a mountain cave. The daughters, believing there were no other men left, got their father drunk with wine to ensure future descendants. The younger daughter gave birth to a son she named Ben-Ammi – a Hebrew name meaning 'son of my people'. Through him an entire nation arose: the Ammonites, who settled east of the Jordan River and established an independent kingdom with Rabbat-Ammon (present-day Amman in Jordan) as its capital. In biblical context, Ben-Ammi's origin shows the complex kinship between the Ammonites and Israel – both connected through Abraham and Lot. Although the Ammonites often stood in opposition to Israel throughout Old Testament history, their right to their land was recognized by God as an inheritance given to Lot's descendants.

keyEvents.title: Birth in the mountain caves after fleeing Sodom
keyEvents.description: After Lot and his daughters fled from Sodom, they settled in a cave in the mountains because Lot feared staying in Zoar. Lot's daughters, believing there were no other men left on earth, got their father drunk with wine to ensure descendants. The younger daughter became pregnant and gave birth to a son she named Ben-Ammi, meaning 'son of my people'. His brother Moab was born from the older daughter.

keyEvents.title: Ancestor of the Ammonites
keyEvents.description: Ben-Ammi became the ancestor of the Ammonites (Hebrew: בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן, bene ammon, 'sons of Ammon'), a people who settled east of the Jordan River in the area around what is now central Jordan. They developed into an independent nation with their own culture, religion, and kingdom, with Rabbah-Ammon as their capital.

keyEvents.title: God's protection of the Ammonite territory
keyEvents.description: When the Israelites were traveling toward the Promised Land, they were explicitly instructed by God not to attack or provoke the Ammonites, because God had given this land to Lot's descendants as their possession. This shows that the kinship between Israel and the Ammonites through Abraham and Lot was recognized.

versions.summary: Ammon was the youngest son of Lot, born through an incestuous relationship with his younger daughter after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. He became the ancestor of the Ammonites, a people who later became enemies of Israel for much of the Old Testament.
versions.title: The Ancestor of the Ammonites
versions.reason: [minor] The title is accurate but could be more descriptive by including the name Ben-Ammi, which is the actual name used in the Bible.; [major] Ammon (Ben-Ammi) was the son of Lot's youngest daughter, not his youngest son. Moab was the son of the eldest daughter, and Ben-Ammi was the son of the youngest. The text says "the youngest son of Lot," which is misleading—Lot had only these two sons, and Ben-Ammi was the one born last (by the youngest daughter), but the wording should be clarified.; [major] The mother of Ammon/Ben-Ammi is known as Lot's youngest daughter. Although she does not have a named ID, this field should not be null. It should be set to a descriptive value or an ID representing her.; [minor] The verse references jump from verse 30 to 36. Important intermediate verses (31–35) are missing, which describe the actual events where the daughters got Lot drunk with wine. Verse 36 mentions that both daughters became pregnant, while verses 37–38 name the sons. The range should be more complete.; [minor] Deuteronomy 2:37 concerns Israel avoiding the land of the Ammonites, but verses 19 and 2:37 are most relevant. Verse 19 is correct. Verse 37 specifically refers to avoiding the border of the Ammonites. The references are acceptable, but verses 19–21 provide a more complete picture.; [minor] The role "patriarch" is somewhat imprecise for someone primarily known as an ancestor of an enemy people. The role "ancestor" would be more accurate. Additionally, "eponym" (namesake of a people) could have been a relevant role.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are important historical, archaeological, and linguistic details about the Ammonites that should be covered: the etymology of Ben-Ammi, archaeological findings from Ammonite culture, and their capital Rabbat-Ammon (today's Amman in Jordan).

versions.summary: Ben-Ammi (also called Ammon) was the son of Lot and his youngest daughter, born through an incestuous relationship after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. According to the account, Lot's two daughters believed that the world had ended, and they got their father drunk with wine to ensure descendants. The younger daughter gave birth to Ben-Ammi, a name meaning "son of my people." He became the ancestor of the Ammonites, a people who settled east of the Jordan River with Rabbah-Ammon (today's Amman) as their capital. Throughout much of the Old Testament, the Ammonites were in a tense relationship with Israel—as neighbors, enemies, and at times also through marital ties to the royal house of Israel.

versions.reason: [minor] The title is good, but Ben-Ammi was born after they settled in a cave – that is precise enough as it stands.; [major] Genesis 19:37 concerns Moab (the son of the older daughter), while verse 38 concerns Ben-Ammi (the son of the younger daughter). The event regarding Ben-Ammi's birth is specifically in verse 38, but verses 30-38 cover the entire context, so it is acceptable to include all. However, it is important to note that verse 37 deals with Moab, not Ben-Ammi.; [major] The mother of Ben-Ammi was Lot's youngest daughter. Although she does not have her own biblical name, the field should not be left blank – it should indicate her identity as 'Lot's-youngest-daughter' or similar to distinguish her from Moab's mother (the older daughter).; [minor] The footnote refers to Deuteronomy 23:4, but the correct verse mentioning Ammonites varies between numbering systems (23:3-4 in the Hebrew text versus 23:4 in other traditions). The reference should be clarified. Furthermore, the prohibition in Deuteronomy 23:4 specifically concerns Ammonites and Moabites, which is correctly stated.; [minor] The footnote mentions that Ruth was from Moab as 'descendants of Ben-Ammi's brother'. Technically, Moab was Ben-Ammi's half-brother (both were sons of Lot, but with different mothers – the older and younger daughters). The phrasing 'half-brother' would have been more precise. Otherwise, the theological observation about Naamah as an Ammonite woman and mother of Rehoboam is highly relevant and correct.; [minor] The summary is well-written and informative. It covers the origin, the meaning of the name, and the further history of the Ammonites in a good way. A small improvement could be to clarify that it was the youngest daughter who was Lot's youngest daughter (not just 'the youngest daughter'), but this is already clear from the context.; [minor] The roles 'patriarch' and 'eponym' are correct. One might consider adding the role 'founder of a people' to clarify that he founded an entire nation, but 'patriarch' covers this sufficiently.

versions.summary: Ben-Ammi (also called Ammon) was the son of Lot and his youngest daughter, conceived through an incestuous relationship after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. When Lot and his two daughters had taken refuge in a mountain cave following the disaster, the daughters believed there were no other men left on earth. To ensure descendants, they got their father drunk with wine. The younger daughter became pregnant and gave birth to a son she named Ben-Ammi, a name meaning 'son of my people'. He became the ancestor of the Ammonites – a people who settled east of the Jordan River with Rabbah-Ammon (present-day Amman in Jordan) as their capital. The Ammonites developed into an independent kingdom with its own religion and culture. Throughout much of Old Testament history, the Ammonites maintained a tense relationship with Israel as neighboring people and frequent opponents, but also through marital ties to the royal house of Israel, such as when the Ammonite Naamah became the mother of King Rehoboam.

footnotes.text: The name Ben-Ammi (בֶּן־עַמִּי) literally means 'son of my people' or 'son of my kinsman'. This name serves as an etiological explanation for the origin of the Ammonites and their kinship with Israel through Lot, Abraham's nephew.

The capital of the Ammonites was Rabbah-Ammon (also called Rabbah), located where the Jordanian capital Amman stands today. The name Amman is a direct continuation of the ancient name Ammon, making it one of the oldest continuously used place names in the world.

Archaeological findings show that the Ammonites developed their own culture with distinctive pottery, sculptures, and inscriptions from around the 10th century BC. Ammonite seals and inscriptions have been found in large numbers in the area surrounding present-day Amman.

In the Old Testament, the Ammonites are consistently portrayed as enemies of Israel. They are mentioned in connection with conflicts during the period of the judges (Judg 10–11), King Saul's time (1 Sam 11), and David's wars (2 Sam 10–12). The law in Deuteronomy 23:4 forbids Ammonites from being admitted into the assembly of the Lord.

Despite the ban on Ammonites joining the assembly, Naamah, an Ammonite woman, was the mother of King Rehoboam (1 Kgs 14:21). Ruth from Moab – descendants of Ben-Ammi's half-brother Moab – became the ancestress of King David. This shows that boundaries between ethnic groups were not always absolute in practice.

According to rabbinic tradition, Lot's daughters' actions are interpreted with some ambivalence. Some rabbis believed the daughters acted in good faith because they thought the whole world had been destroyed (as in Noah's time), while others condemned the act. The Talmud (Horayot 10b) discusses the intentions and motives of the older daughter.

The deity of the Ammonites was Milcom (also called Molech), who is mentioned several times in the Old Testament. King Solomon built a high place for Milcom in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 11:5,33), which was considered a serious sin. Archaeological findings from the region confirm the central role of the Milcom cult in Ammonite religion.

The term 'Ammonites' in Hebrew is בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן (bene ammon), which literally means 'sons/children of Ammon'. This patronymic naming practice was common among Semitic peoples in the ancient Levant, where entire ethnic groups were identified through their ancestor.
